IS 15350 : 2003 

Indian Standard 

AUTOMOTIVE VEHICLES — IGNITION 
SYSTEMS — METHODS OF TEST 



ICS 43.060.50 



O BiS2003 

BUREAU OF INDIAN STANDARDS 

MANAK BHAVAN, 9 BAHADUR SHAH ZAFAR MARG 
NEW DELHI 110002 

June 2003 Price Group 6 



Automotive Electrical Equipment Sectional Committee, TED 1 1 



FOREWORD 

This Indian Standard was adopted by the Bureau of Indian Standards, after the draft finalized by the 
Automotive Electrical Equipment Sectional Committee had been approved by the Transport Engineering 
Division Council. 

This standard is intended to aid the designers and users of ignition systems of automotive vehicles fitted with 
spark ignition engines. 

While preparing thi^ standard considerable assistance has been derived from ISO 65 1 8-2 : 199S 'Road vehicles — 
Ignitions systems — Part 2 : Electrical performance and function test methods'. 

The standard outlines two methods for calculating the system output energy because of difficulties in repeatability 
of results with atmospheric spark gaps and different observers. 

The composition of the Committee responsible for the formulation of this standard is given in Annex A. 

For the purpose of deciding whether a particular requirement of this standard is complied with, the final 
value, observed or calculated, expressing the result of a test or analysis, shall be rounded off in accordance with 
IS 2 : I960 'Rules for rounding off numerical values ( revised)\ The number of significant places retained in the 
rounded off value should be the same as that of the specified value in this standard. 



IS 15350 : 2003 



Indian Standard 

AUTOMOTIVE VEHICLES — IGNITION 
SYSTEMS — METHODS OF TEST 



1 SCOPE 



This standard specifies the conditions and test 
methods for testing ignition systems of automotive 
vehicles for four wheelers with reference to their 
electrical performance. 

2 IGNITION SYSTEMS DESCRIPTION 

For the tests described in the standard, the ignition 
system components used shall be as specified for the 
application being examined and shall be in accordance 
with the original equipment specification. 



The following components shall be interconnected 
as shown in Fig. 1(a) or in any other circuit which has 
been proved to be equivalent. 

2.1.1 Single-Ended Coil 

Conventional induction coil or an air/magnetic core 
transformer. 

2.1.2 Coil Ballast Resistor(s) 

if the coil being tested requires a ballast resistor, or 
any fixed or variable means to make the voltage and/ 
or the current in the ignition circuit vary. 

2.1.3 Distributor 

It distributes the ignition impulses to the spark plugs, 
it may also contain means of triggering and/or timing 
adjustment, all of which have a proper angular 
interrelationship to themselves and to the engine. 

2.1.4 Auxiliary Switching Device 

implicit with the system being tested such as a 
transistorized control unit. 

2.2 Static ( Distributorless ) Ignition System with 
Single-Ended Coils 

The following components shall be interconnected 
as shown in Fig. 1(b) or in any other circuit which 
has been proved to be equivalent. 

2.2.1 Coils 

Depending on the system tested, the coils may be: 

a) Single-ended coils as described in 2.1.1, or 

b) A multiple high-tension terminal assembly 
formed by single ended coils, or 



c) Plug-top coils. 

2.2.2 Auxiliary Switching Device 

Implicit with the system being tested such as a 
transistorized control unit. 

2.3 Static ( Distributorless ) Ignition System with 
Double-Ended Coil(s) 

The following components shall be interconnected 
as shown in Fig. 1(c) or in any other circuit which has 
proved to be equivalent. 



2.1 Ignition System with Mechanical Distributor 2.3.1 Coils 



Depending on the system tested, the coils may be: 

a) Double-ended coils, or 

b) A multiple high-tension terminal assembly 
formed by double-ended coils. 

2.3.2 Auxiliary Switching Device 

Implicit with the system being tested such as a 
transistorized control unit. 

3 TEST EQUIPMENT 

3.1 Variable d.c. Power Supply 

A d.c. source which shall be a variable d.c. power 
supply having a 10 percent to 90 percent transient 
recovery time of not more than SO ^s over the load 
range encountered in use. It shall have not more than 
50 mV variation in average voltage from no-load to 
full ignition system load and not more than 100 mV 
peak-to-peak ripple over the same load range. This 
power supply may be substituted by a battery with 
or without a charging system. The power supply shall 
be positioned immediately adjacent to the system being 
tested. 

3.2 Oscilloscope 

An oscilloscope with a maximum rise time of 35 ns, 
with a minimum band pass of 10 MHz shall be used 
( P^ and ^2 )• The overall uncertainty of measurement 
including voltage and current probes ( see 3.3 
and 3.4 ) shall be less than 3 percent. 

3.3 Voltage Probe, i7p 

With an input capacitance smaller than or equal 
to 5 pF and an input resistance of 100 MQ or greater.

3.4 Current Probe, P, 

Suitable for d.c. to 1 MHz. 

3.5 d.c. Ammeter, P^ 

With a maximum voltage drop of 100 mV under test 
conditions. 

3.6 Voltmeter, P^ 

With an input resistance of at least 10 KQ/V and with 
sufficient resolution to easily indicate differences of 
10 mV easily. 

3.7 Distributor or Trigger Wheel Drive Stand and 
Attached Tachometer {P^)^ conforming to the 
following: 

a) A continuously variable rotational frequency 
adjustment, capable of being varied between 
1 min ' and 4 000 min"' for a distributor drive 
stand and between 20 min"* and at least 
6 000 min~' for a trigger wheel drive stand; 

b) The rotational frequency shall be within 
± 5 percent below 400 min ' and ± 20 min"' 
above 400 min'; and 

c) A tachometer accurate to within ± 0.2 percent 
of indicated rotational frequency. 

3.8 Loads shall be connected to the ignition system 
by high voltage, non-resistive metal conductor ignition 
cables. The length depends on the capacitive load 
( see 3.8.2 ). 

3.8.1 Multi-Point Spark Gap Stand 

Each gap being individually variable ( see Fig. 3 ). 

3.8.2 Capacitance, C, 

Simulates the capacitance of the cables and spark 
plugs as normally encountered on the engine. This 
capacitance shall be a low dissipation factor ( not greater 
than 3 percent at 1 kHz ) secondary ignition cable 
of a length of 4S0 mm between coil to distributor 
and 600 mm between distributor/coil to spark gaps 
such that in conjunction with the capacitor and high 
tension probe the total capacitance is: 

a) SO pF to 55 pF for ignition systems with 
distributor; 

b) 25 pF to 30 pF for static ignition systems with 
single-ended coils; and 

c) 50 pF to 55 pF for static ignition systems with 
single-ended coils. 

NOTES 

1 For measuring the total capacitance, the distributor 
spark gaps and the impedances R2io R^q, if lumped 
resistors, shall be shunted and the ignition cable shall 
be removed from the ignition coil. 



2 It may be necessary to consider the effect of parasitic 
capacitances. 

3 Other values of capacitance may be agreed upon 
depending on the application. 

3.8.3 Resistor, /?, 

Simulates lead or carbon fouled spark plugs. This 
resistor shall have a low voltage coefficient 
( 0.000 5 percent/V,,^), non-inductive, approximately 
10 W and I Mil ± 5 percent. It shall be connected in 
parallel to the capacitance for some measurements. 

3.8.4 A zener diode string of 1 kV for single-ended 
coils and two Zener diode strings of 1 kV and 0.5 kV 
for double ended coils [ see Fig. 1(c) ], each with a 
Zener voltage tolerance of i: 5 percent under test 
conditions. 

4 PARAMETERS TO BE MEASURED OR 
DETERMINED 

4.1 Available Voltage, U^^ 

Comparing the available voltage U^^ to the voltage 
required U^^^, to fire spark-plugs ( in a given 
engine ) determines the adequacy of the ignition 
system [ see Fig. 2 (a) ]. It shall be measured when 
the system is loaded with the capacitance C, described 
in 3.8.2. 

4.2 Minimum Available Voltage, U^^^ 

This voltage shall be measured when the system is 
loaded with the capacitance C^ and the resistor R^ 
connected in parallel. The minimum amplitude shall 
be recorded. This represents the level which can be 
guaranted from the system being tested at an 
ambient temperature of 23°C ± 5°C, a trigger wheel 
rotational frequency of 2 000 min~^ and a supply voltage 
of 13.5 V 

4.3 Secondary Output Voltage, U^ 

The secondary output voltage U^ may also be measured 
for comparison with values obtained for available 
voltage U^^. 

4.4 Interruption Current,/ . 

This parameter determines the energy into the system 
[see Fig. 2(0)1 

NOTE — This measurement is not applicable to capacitor 
discharge ignition systems. 

4.5 Average Current Input, /p^^ 

This parameter determines the average current draw 
of the system with respect to the d.c.sources such 
as alternator, generator, battery. 

4.6 Energy 

4.6.1 Inductive Spark Energy, £ . 

The inductive spark energy £ ■ is determined by

4.6.3 Spark Duration or Zener Discharge Duration 

This parameter within limits is indicative of the igniting 
capability of the ignition coil output und^r conditions 
as agreed to between the manufacturer and the 
purchaser [ see Fig 2 (d), (0 and (g) ]. 

NOTE — It is an indication of the amount of erosion 
which occurs on spark-plug electrodes due to electrical 
means. Experience is required to use this information 
effectively. 

4.6.4 Maximum Spark Current, / or Maximum Zener 
Discharge Current, I^^^ 

This current is the instantaneous current from 
the secondary winding of the ignition coil flowing 
through the spark gap after break down [ see Fig. 2(0 ] 
or through the Zener diodes [ see Fig. 2(g) ]. 

NOTES 

1 This measurement is not applicable to capacitor 
discharge ignition systems. 

2 It is an indication of the amount of erosion which 
occurs on spark-plug electrodes due to electrical means. 
Experience is required to use this information 
effectively. 

4.7 Secondary Voltage Rise Time, /,^^ 

This parameter is an indication of the ability of an 
ignition system to fire shunted ( fouled ) spark 
plugs. The shorter the secondary voltage rise time, 
the less system energy is lost across the fouled shunt 
and more voltage is available to fire the spark plug 
[5^^ Fig. 2(b)]. 



It shall be measured when the system is loaded with 
the capacitance C, described in 3.8.2 and the resistor 
/;, described in 3.8.3. 

To facilitate comparison between systems, the 
secondary voltage rise time shall be determined between 
-1 .5 kV and -1 5 kV to be repeated between +1 .5 kV 
and + 1 S kV for double-ended coils or as agreed between 
the user and the manufacturer. 

4.8 Coil Primary Induced Voltage, U^^^ 

This parameter is useful with respect to contact 
breaker life in classical ignition systems and is an 
indication of the stress on a semiconductor power 
switch ( unless voltage clamping is used ) in inductive 
energy storage ignition systems [ see Fig. 2(e) ]. If it 
shall be measured, it may be necessary to use a 
measuring instrument with a differential input. 

NOTES 

1 This measurement is not applicable to capacitor discharge 
ignition systems. 

2 The primary induced voltage wave form is always 
preceded ( usually within 20 fis ) by a leakage induction 
spike. Usually this is ignored in calculations but if the 
area under the '"spike" curve becomes significant then 
it is essential that it be taken into account, when 
considering the effect on solid state components. 

4.9 Ignition Limiting Load Resistance, it|3,^y 

The shunt behaviour of an ignition system is also 
determined by its ignition limiting load resistance. It 
is the resistance at which the absolute value of the 
available voltage falls to I S kV. The designation for it 
is R^^yy [ see /?, in Fig. 1(a) to 1(c) ]. 

The parameter are C^^^ [ see C, in Fig. 1(a) to 1(c) ] 
as described in 3.8.2. 

^supply = ^3.5 V; 

'^crankshaft = ZOOOmin"'. 

5 PROCEDURES 

5.1 General 

The circuit arrangements shown in Fig. 1(a) to 1(c) 
with instrumentation in place can be used to measure 
the parameters mentioned in 4. Test arrangement A 
is intended for test to confirm the required system 
functions and system performance. 

Test arrangement B is intended for tests to compare 
the performance of ignition coils and current interruption 
systems. 

5.2 Test Conditions 

The test conditions shall be chosen from Table 1 as 
appropriate.

During simulated starting tests, the system shall be 
operated under conditions simulating vehicle electrical 
conditions for the primary side of the system. For 
example, if a resistor in series with the primary coil is 
normally shunted during vehicle cranking, this resistor 
shall be shunted for this portion of bench tests. 

5.2.1 Supply Voltage, U^^^ 

The supply voltages U^^^^ given in Table 1 are based 
on 12 V nominal voltage. If 24 V systems are to be 
tested, multiply these voltages by two. 

5.2.2 Ambient Temperatures 

Allow the ignition system to soak at least one hour 
at the temperatures listed in Table I before beginning 
of the tests. 

Before any reading are recorded at any of the test points, 
the system should be allowed to come to a thermally 
stable operating condition to be agreed upon between 
the manufacturer and the user. 

When environmental equipment is used to control 
ambient temperatures, care shall be taken that wire 
and/or cable lengths and, consequently, impedances 
do not distort test results. 

5.3 Test Methods 

The test methods A and B differ in the test arrange- 
ment for the energy measurement ( spark voltage or 



Zener discharge voltage, spark current or Zener 
discharge current and spark duration or 21ener discharge 
duration ). The resulting calculated energies are also 
likely to difTer. 

5.3.1 Test Method A ( Inductive Spark Energy ) 

Test method A is closest to a vehicle installation 
and shall be used with test arrangement A to confirm 
the system functions. It shall be used to measure 
the parameters mentioned in 4 under the conditions 
listed in 5.2 under the appropriate conditions of 
Table I. 

The calculation described in 4.6.1 with the procedure 
described here determines the inductive part of the 
spark energy discharged in a spark gap as shown in 
Fig. 3 and Fig. 4. The spark gap for single-ended coils 
shall be set to give a spark voltage U^of \ kV ± 5 
percent. For double-ended coils [ see Fig. 1(c) ] two 
spark gaps shall be used, one set to 1 kV ± S percent, 
the other to 0.5 kV d: 5 percent, for each secondary 
winding. 

The oscilloscope P-^ ( see 3.2 ) and the voltage probe 
R^ ( see 3.3 ) shall be used to measure the spark voltage 
and the spark duration. The voltage probe shall be 
connected to a spark gap that has been adjusted to a 
value U , For measuring the spark current a current 
probe shall be used as shown in Fig. 1(a) to 1(c), test 
arrangement A.

5.3.2 Test Method B (Zener Discharge Energy) 

Test method B shall be used with test arrang ement B 
to compare the performance and function of ignition 
coils and current interruption systems. 

For the energy measurement, a Zener diode string of 
1 kV as shown in Fig. 1(a) and 1(b), test arrangement 
B, or one Zener diode string of 1 kV and one Zener 
diode string of 0.5 kV as shown in Fig. 1(c) shall be 
used. The discharge current used for the energy 
calculation shall be measured by using a current probe 
as shown in Fig. 1(a) to 1(c), test arrangement B. 

The energy calculation is described in 4.6.2. 

The oscilloscope P^ and the voltage probe R^ are used 
as shown in Fig. 1(a) to 1(c) to measure the voltage 
across the Zener diode string and the discharge 
duration. 

NOTE — The polarity of the coil secondary to be 
determined before conducting the test to avoid damage 
to the electronic components.

Bureau of Indian Standards 

BIS is a statutory institution established under the Bureau of Indian Standards Act, 1986 to promote 
harmonious development of the activities of standardization, marking and quality certification of goods and 
attending to connected matters in the country. 

Copyright 

B IS has the copyright of all its publications. No part of these publications may be reproduced in any form without 
the prior permission in writing of BIS. This does not preclude the free use, in the course of implementing the 
standard, of necessary details, such as symbols and sizes, type or grade designations. Enquiries relating to 
copyright be addressed to the Director (Publications), BIS. 

Review of Indian Standards 

Amendments are issued to standards as the need arises on the basis of comments. Standards are also reviewed 
periodically; a standard along with amendments is reaffirmed when such review indicates that no changes are 
needed; if the review indicates that changes are needed, it is taken up for revision. Users of Indian Standards 
should ascertain that they are in possession of the latest amendments of edition by referring to the latest issue 
of 'BIS Catalogue' and 'Standards : Monthly Additions'. 

This Indian Standard has been developed from Doc : No. TED 1 1 ( 178 ).
